summary: This RFC discusses the protocols proposed in RFC 914 and RFC 916 and suggests one that could meet the same need: reliable communication between two programs over a point-to-point link, especially slow asynchronous ones.

plainLanguage.summary: Two earlier plans tried to make slow phone-style links reliable. This note compares them and offers a single plan that does the job.

questions: reliable link layer protocols for serial links
character oriented vs bit oriented link protocols
why use crc on serial links
subtitle: A comparison of standard link layer protocols that argues for existing standards instead of new ones on slow asynchronous lines.

tldr.problem: RFCs 914 and 916 proposed new protocols for reliable communication over a point-to-point, often slow asynchronous, serial link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares character-oriented, bit-oriented and DDCMP framing, error checks, sequencing and addressing, then recommends transparent character-oriented framing, a 16-bit CRC and the LAPB control procedures.
tldr.outcome: The recommended protocol costs 8 characters of overhead per frame and allows up to 7 frames outstanding in each direction. The author expects such links to be used only for a relatively short period.

today: The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 935. The author himself predicted that links of this kind would be used for a relatively short period, as X.25 and LAN data links took over.

sections.title: Existing Standards for Serial Links
sections.content:
RFC 935 responds to RFCs 914 and 916, which propose protocols for transferring serial data reliably over asynchronous lines. The author summarizes standards that have long existed and hopes they will meet the same needs.

Serial link layer standards fall into two classes. Character-oriented protocols are older, standardized in ANSI X3.28-1976 and ISO standards such as IS 1745. Bit-oriented protocols are standardized in ADCCP and in ISO HDLC, and are followed by SDLC (IBM), X.25 LAPB (CCITT), IEEE 802.2 LLC and ISDN LAPD. The only other widely used protocol the author knows is DEC's DDCMP, which uses a character count instead of framing characters.
sections.plainLanguage: There are already two old, well-tested ways to send messages along a wire, plus one more from one company. The note compares them before inventing anything new.

sections.title: How Each Protocol Frames Data
sections.content:
All the protocols divide data into frames, and framing is the main difference between the three classes.

Character-oriented protocols mark the start and end of a frame with special framing characters. To allow any data in the frame, transparency is obtained by preceding each framing character with a control character, typically DLE, and doubling DLE when it appears in the data.

Bit-oriented protocols use a FLAG: a 0 bit, six 1 bits, then another 0 bit. The sender inserts an extra 0 after any five successive 1 bits in the data, and the receiver removes it. This makes frame lengths arbitrary in bits, so bit-oriented protocols are generally useful only in synchronous transmission.

DDCMP puts a count field in a fixed-length header that says how many characters of text follow. No framing characters are needed, so transparency is not a problem. But because a bad count breaks synchronization, the header has its own check, and SYN characters must precede each frame even on asynchronous lines.
sections.plainLanguage: Framing is how the receiver knows where one message ends and the next begins. You can use special marker words, special marker patterns, or a number at the front saying how long the message is.

sections.title: Error Detection and Check Sequences
sections.content:
Most synchronous uses attach a 16-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC) to each frame. Hardware can compute it with a shift register; software needs about 5 to 6 instructions per character and a 256 by 16-bit lookup table. DDCMP and the bit-oriented protocols require it, and DDCMP uses one for the header and another for the data. Character-oriented links sometimes use weaker checks: character parity (odd for synchronous and even for asynchronous links per ANSI X3.16-1976) and longitudinal parity.

RFCs 914 and 916 use simple additive and exclusive-or checks. The author calls both relatively weak compared to CRC techniques. IP and TCP already carry checksums, but recovering at the TCP layer is slow on noisy links, and the link control field needs protection against needless loss or duplication of frames. A CRC combined with the additive IP and TCP checks gives much more protection than two additive checks, because the techniques address different kinds of errors.
sections.plainLanguage: A check number lets the receiver notice scrambled messages. A stronger check number catches more mistakes than a simple adding-up check.

sections.title: Sequencing, Acknowledgments and Addressing
sections.content:
All the protocols give reliability by numbering frames and using positive and, in some cases, negative acknowledgments. Character-oriented protocols implicitly number frames and allow one outstanding, or up to 7 if frames are explicitly numbered. Bit-oriented protocols number frames explicitly and allow up to 7 outstanding, or up to 127 with the control field extension. DDCMP allows up to 255 outstanding.

Addressing lets stations on a multipoint link be addressed separately. Addresses are typically one character, though bit-oriented protocols allow longer ones, and character-oriented protocols use two-character addresses. For point-to-point operation the address is superfluous, except that bit-oriented protocols use it to tell commands from replies.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages get numbers so the receiver can say which ones arrived. Addresses are like names on envelopes, which matter little when only two people share the wire.

sections.title: Comparing Overhead on a Slow Line
sections.content:
The author compares overhead in characters per frame, including RATP (from RFC 916) for contrast. For framing, check and transparency the totals are 8 for character-oriented, 5 for bit-oriented, 8 for DDCMP and 5 for RATP. Transparency costs depend on the data: about one DLE per 256-byte frame on average for character-oriented protocols, but 256 in the worst case.

Bit-oriented framing suits only synchronous links, so the author drops it, and prefers character-oriented framing for its wide use and chip support. For control, address and acknowledgment, bit-oriented procedures cost the least among public standards (2 characters), and there is no conflict using them on asynchronous links. The author recommends LAPB, the best known of that family.

For 13-byte frames, the minimum for Thinwire II in RFC 914, 8 characters of overhead is 61% versus 46% for RATP's 6 characters. On a 1200 baud line, which is 120 characters per second, that is 74 versus 82 characters per second. The RFC concludes RATP saves little, and that for larger frames the extra 2 characters per frame fall to a few percent or less.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message needs a little wrapping. The note counts the wrapping for each method and finds the old standard wraps only slightly more than the new idea.

sections.title: The Recommended Protocol
sections.content:
For asynchronous dial-up communication between PCs, the author advocates transparent, character-oriented framing, a 16-bit CRC and the LAPB control procedures. The CRC should be CRC-16 or the CCITT CRC used in X.25, with the latter preferred. The frame format is DLE STX <control and data ...> DLE ETX CRC CRC.

Overhead is 8 characters per frame, and up to 7 frames may be outstanding in each direction. The author thinks IP datagrams are acceptable frames for 1200 baud dial-up service. Dropping the one-character address or using RATP's count-oriented frame would save a little, but is not recommended because it departs from common practice.

The author also expects X.25 to become the protocol of choice, so links like these will likely be used only for a relatively short period, with the future being LAN or X.25/X.32 link layers, X.25 and/or ISO IP, and TCP and/or ISO TP4.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice: use the proven old rules for the wire, use a strong check number, and let the sender have a few messages in flight at once.
